title: Scroll-triggered animation support in static prerendering
subtitle: Prerender script now simulates full-page scrolling to trigger framer-motion animations before capture
facts: Prerender script scrolls entire page in viewport-height increments with 120ms delays between scrolls
Waits for animations to complete by checking for remaining elements with inline opacity: 0
Ensures below-the-fold content is fully rendered before HTML capture for crawler visibility
Returns to top (scroll position 0) after animations settle before final HTML capture
narrative: Added scroll simulation logic to the prerender Puppeteer script to trigger framer-motion's whileInView animations during static HTML capture. The script scrolls through the page in viewport-height/2 increments, pausing 120ms between each scroll to allow animations to fire. After reaching the bottom, it waits 600ms then scrolls back to top. Before capturing HTML, it validates that all scroll-triggered reveals completed by checking that no visible DOM elements still have `opacity: 0` styling. This solves a critical SEO issue where below-the-fold animated content would be serialized with hidden opacity states, making it invisible to non-JavaScript crawlers that don't scroll. The warning fallback logs if some elements remain hidden at capture time.
author: mail@maxritter.net

title: Prefers-reduced-motion accessibility support
subtitle: App now respects user's OS motion preferences via framer-motion MotionConfig
facts: Automatically respects system prefers-reduced-motion media query setting
Animations skip or execute instantly for users with reduced motion enabled
Global configuration applies to all framer-motion animations across all routes
narrative: Added accessibility support for motion-sensitive users by wrapping the app in framer-motion's MotionConfig component with `reducedMotion="user"`. This setting respects the `prefers-reduced-motion` media query from the user's operating system, which is enabled when users configure motion reduction in their accessibility settings (common for users with vestibular disorders, ADHD, or other motion-triggered discomfort). When active, framer-motion disables all animations and transitions, executing state changes instantly instead. The global configuration ensures consistent behavior across all animated components, pages, and transitions without requiring per-component configuration.

Below the bars sits a role row mapping career positions across those same years, making the evolution from first engineer through to five-year freelance tenure visible as a diagram rather than prose. The three color schemes test different visual hierarchies: (3a) uses a single amber accent for restraint, (3b) splits history (cyan) from current work (amber) to show continuity with change, and (3c) assigns each era its own hue for maximum visual distinction. All three use oklch color space with consistent accent application across UI elements (navigation state, hover effects, status tags). The design avoids naming the co-founded startup, per user guidance, and surfaces six key clients and three personal projects (Pilot Shell framework, Bahnsparer fare-watcher app, DIY-Thermocam open-source thermal camera).

title: Four visual design directions proposed for website redesign
subtitle: Systems Line recommended; three challengers (Street Signal, Contact Sheet, Instrument Bench) each with complete visual grammar and risk profile
facts: Systems Line (recommended): urban transit/systems architecture language; cobalt field, cream, coral, lime palette; connects roles/industries/domains through unified route diagram metaphor

Street Signal (challenger): wood-type public theater posters; yellow, black, paper white, red-orange palette; makes "ADVISE, ARCHITECT, BUILD" a typographic public statement; risks reading as agency branding rather than individual expert

Contact Sheet (challenger): hand-processed 16mm film and edit-room contact sheets; silver-gray, cream, orange, brown palette; unfolds career as frame-by-frame visual narrative; risks making present-day offer less immediate

Instrument Bench (challenger): nixie laboratory counters and calibrated instruments; black, orange, metal gray, dark blue palette; treats roles and domains as calibrated modes on an instrument panel; risks reading as retro-technical gadgetry

Canonical option (Executive Portfolio): industry-standard conservative alternative with quiet editorial grid, clean portrait, and precise case-study cards; immediately credible but less able to make technical range memorable
Each direction includes specific palette, materials, viewport composition, responsive behavior, and explicit risk assessment
narrative: direction-options.json documents four complete visual design systems for the website redesign. Systems Line (the recommended direction) draws from urban transit schematics and systems architecture diagrams, using a large cobalt field to position Max's portrait and current offer alongside a living route diagram that visualizes the progression from strategic advisory work through shipped systems—metaphorically treating his career as one connected engineering system. Street Signal employs architectural wood-type typography and public theater poster language to make his three core activities (ADVISE, ARCHITECT, BUILD) into a visual manifesto, but carries the risk of theatrical force that could overshadow the technical proof. Contact Sheet uses hand-processed 16mm film strips and edit-room contact sheets to tell the career as a continuous body of work unfolding frame-by-frame, which beautifully carries the narrative arc but delays the present-day offer. Instrument Bench treats roles and technical domains as calibrated operating modes on a precision laboratory instrument panel, which resonates immediately with engineers but may signal "retro tooling" to business decision-makers. Each includes a risk assessment (e.g., Systems Line requires the map to remain evidence-driven navigation, not decorative infographic noise). A canonical Executive Portfolio option is documented as the standing industry default: a restrained editorial layout with portrait, value statement, client proof strip, and clear contact action—reliable but less differentiating.

title: Empty interface lint errors fixed in shadcn components
subtitle: Converted empty interface definitions to type aliases in command and textarea components
facts: src/components/ui/command.tsx: interface CommandDialogProps extends DialogProps {} → type CommandDialogProps = DialogProps
Pattern addresses pre-existing empty-interface ESLint violations in shadcn-generated code
narrative: Empty interface definitions in shadcn/ui components were causing ESLint warnings. These were replaced with equivalent type alias syntax (interface X extends Y {} → type X = Y), which is the recommended pattern for interfaces that only extend without adding members. This is a common TypeScript best practice for reducing boilerplate and improving code consistency.

title: Complete editorial redesign of maxritter.net shipped with new visual identity
subtitle: Dark palette, custom typography, 4-page editorial layout with SEO and cross-project references
facts: Color palette: dark near-black background (#0a0b0d) + amber primary (hsl 34 91% 60%) + cyan accent
Typography: self-hosted Switzer font (weights 300–700) + Geist Mono; fonts hosted in public/fonts
Layout approach: no-cards, hairline-rule editorial design (replaces old component-based ProductsSection, HeroSection, SkillsSection, etc.)

Four pages shipped: Index (hero + NOW line + clients + project index), Projects (per-product detail with anchors), Work (nine years/five hats, 12 engagements from src/data/work.ts), Skills (from src/data/skills.ts)
SEO: Person schema with workExample SoftwareApplications + images; ItemList + BreadcrumbList on subpages; em-dashes stored as unicode escapes in JSX
ScrollManager in App.tsx handles hash anchor navigation with retry loop; AnimatePresence delays mount to prevent whileInView flickering during prerender
Prerender script scrolls page to ensure whileInView content renders at full opacity, never captured at 0
Design iterated through 5 versions in Claude Design project (v1 serif rejected, v2 grotesque, v3 colors, v4 all pages, v5 home approved)
narrative: A full editorial redesign replaced the previous component-heavy architecture with a cohesive dark-palette layout. The color strategy (dark background with amber primary and cyan accent) drives visual hierarchy across all pages. Typography uses self-hosted Switzer for headlines/body and Geist Mono for code/details, supporting the editorial voice. The Index page opens with a condensed hero and client list; Projects page offers per-product detail with side anchors (e.g., #pilot-shell); Work page chronicles nine years across five roles with 12 timestamped engagements; Skills page pulls structured data. SEO is layered with Person schema, workExample metadata, and breadcrumbs to surface project cross-references. Technical decisions include unicode-escaped em-dashes for charset compliance, ScrollManager for hash-anchor navigation with retry logic, and a prerender pass that scrolls the page so whileInView animations render at full opacity. This represents a complete departure from the old ProductsSection/HeroSection component model in favor of a unified editorial system.
